大正琴屬日本弦鳴樂器，來源未載持琴姿勢；發聲依靠琴鍵控制弦長，旋律弦以鍵盤按壓後: The taishōgoto is a Japanese chordophone; the source does not record how the instrument is held. It sounds by using keys to control the length of the strings: the melody strings are stopped with the keyboard and then plucked, and there are also drone strings, usually tuned to D, whose pitch cannot be changed while playing. A beginner can first turn the pegs with a tuning key, then press the two rows of keys with the left hand while the right hand uses a pick, or a false nail, to pluck from one side of the strings to the other. For a long note, pluck quickly back and forth to make a tremolo; the strings can also be rebounded or bowed. A slide is not possible on the modern instrument.

The taishōgoto is a Japanese chordophone, also called the Nagoya harp and known in Taiwan as the zhongshan qin, Hornbostel–Sachs number 314.122-8. The body is a hollow wooden box fitted with a simple keyboard and several metal strings, with melody strings and drone strings; the player presses keys with the left hand to change pitch and plucks with a pick or a false nail in the right hand. Because it is simple to build and easy to play it was popular as a household instrument; it has also been used in krautrock (Krautrock) recordings, by benshi film narrators and in teaching programmes.
大正琴為弦鳴樂器，右手撥弦、左手按鍵改變音高。旋律弦通常調為G音的不同八度，另有: The taishōgoto is a chordophone: the right hand plucks the strings and the left hand presses keys to change pitch. The melody strings are usually tuned to Gs in different octaves, and there is one drone string on D whose pitch cannot be changed while playing. The strings are mostly steel wire, and two octaves can sound at once; because the strings differ in thickness, a plucked string gives a short note that has overtones and resonance and is described as bright. The range depends on the number of keys, at least 12 to 34 notes; early instruments covered about two octaves and later ones came in lower-pitched types. The source does not describe how volume is controlled. The principle is close to keyed string instruments in India, Pakistan and Germany, but the Swedish nyckelharpa strikes its strings differently.
大正琴為日本弦鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 314.122-8，以鍵: The taishōgoto is a Japanese chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 314.122-8, sounded by stopping strings with a keyboard and plucking with the right hand. It was popular as a household instrument and also appeared in primary and secondary school music lessons, radio programmes and Japanese educational television; the film narrator Yamazaki Masami also used a taishōgoto. On record, the source mentions a German rock band using one on its 1972 debut album, and another band that used it too. It has also been performed in India, Southeast Asia and Kenya.
大正琴琴身為扁長方形中空共鳴箱，面板常用雲杉或唐檜，側板見楓木、毛泡桐、櫸木、刺: The body of the taishōgoto is a flat rectangular hollow resonating box. The soundboard is usually spruce or Japanese hinoki, the sides are maple, paulownia, zelkova or black locust, and the fretboard is rosewood or ebony. Inside the cavity, wooden bars and posts brace the frame and the bridge; hardwood is glued into the head to take the tuning pegs. The sounding body is the metal strings, recorded in the source as steel wire, some of them wound to give a lower octave and harmony; the pegs are made of thin iron rod. The keys are mostly stamped from sheet metal, with note names inlaid or lettered on the buttons, and some are plastic; the damper board and key plate are wooden. The materials of the remaining parts are not stated.
大正琴（Taishōgoto）於1912年由森田吾郎在名古屋創製，以二弦琴為基礎: The taishōgoto was created in Nagoya in 1912 by Morita Gorō, built on a two-string zither and inspired by the typewriter keyboard, with a key order close to the piano's. It began with two strings and two octaves, and because it was simple and easy to play it became a popular household instrument in the Taishō era. Strings and keys were added later, and in the 1970s and 1980s alto, tenor and bass models appeared, along with the electric taishōgoto, models played on a strap and variants such as the Shōwa koto. The instrument also reached India, Southeast Asia and Kenya, and a German rock band used one in 1972. In China it was named zhongshan qin in memory of the Republic of China and Sun Yat-sen, and several schools and associations formed around it.
